s: weight
obsolete
massiveness, bulkiness, bulk
Die Wucht der Kasernenbauten steht in scharfem Kontrast zu den umliegenden Reihenhäuschen.
The massiveness of the barracks buildings is in sharp contrast to the surrounding terraced houses.
force, momentum of a moving mass
Der Krater zeugt von der Wucht des Einschlags.
The crater attests to the force of the impact.
force, impetus, the sudden accumulation of power into a motion
Du solltest die Hantel nicht mit Wucht hochziehen, sondern langsam nach oben drücken.
You should not lift the dumbbell with force, but rather push it up slowly.
stunning, powerful effect on the mind etc.
figuratively
Die Nachricht von ihrem Tod traf mich mit voller Wucht.
The news of her death struck me with full force.
Erst nach seinem Tod entfalteten seine Attacken auf die christliche Moral oder seine Gedanken zum „Übermenschen“ ihre ganze Wucht.
something great, smashing, rad
dated
informal
Das ist ja ’ne Wucht, dass wir uns hier treffen.
That’s smashing that we ran into each other here.
lifting-jack, lever
obsolete
Wucht.et: 17th century (standard since ca. 1800), from Low German Wucht (“weight”), byform of Wicht with assimilation of the vowel to the adjacent consonants. Further from Middle Low German wicht(e), from Proto-Germanic *wihtiz. Cognate with English weight.

s: growth; growing
form; shape; build (the way something has grown)
Wuchs.et: Deverbal from wachsen (“to grow”), past tense wuchs, by analogy with similar ablaut formations; from the 18th century.

s: usury (loaning at excessive interest rates)
Nach dem Alten Testament ist Wucher verboten.
According to the Old Testament, usury is forbidden.
sale at excessive prices; overpricing, gouging; highway robbery
Vier Euro für ein kleines Bier, das ist doch Wucher!
Four euros for a small beer, that's totally overpriced!
Wucher.et: From Middle High German wuocher, from Old High German wuohhar, from Proto-Germanic *wōkraz. Compare Dutch woeker, English oker.

s: usurer (one who loans money at exorbitant interest rates), loan shark
Wucherer.et: From Middle High German wuocherære, from Old High German wuohharāri, derived from wuohhar, whence modern German Wucher (“usury”).
